qs.q: Which management strategy is recommended for a patient diagnosed with acute mastitis during the first month of breastfeeding?
o: Prescribe antibiotics and continue expressing milk
Perform immediate surgical excision of the duct
Administer high-dose systemic corticosteroids
Stop breastfeeding immediately and apply heat packs
qs.e: Treatment for acute mastitis involves antibiotics and continuing to breastfeed or express milk, with surgical drainage reserved only for abscesses that fail to resolve with antibiotics. Stopping breastfeeding is not recommended.
qs.s: Breast Inflammation: Mastitis, Periductal Mastitis & Duct Ectasia: MCQs

qs.q: What is the appropriate primary medical treatment for idiopathic or autoimmune granulomatous mastitis?
o: Topical antifungal creams
Tamoxifen therapy
Corticosteroid therapy
High-dose radiation
qs.e: Steroids are used to treat autoimmune or idiopathic granulomatous mastitis, whereas antibiotics are used if a bacterial cause like Corynebacteria or mycobacteria is identified. Radiation and hormonal therapy play no role in treating inflammatory granulomas of the breast.
qs.s: Breast Inflammation: Mastitis, Periductal Mastitis & Duct Ectasia: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following epidemiological and clinical features distinguishes duct ectasia from periductal mastitis (Zuska disease)?
o: Absence of a strong association with cigarette smoking
Frequent presentation with purulent acute bacterial cellulitis
Occurrence predominantly in younger nulliparous females
Primary manifestation as painful subareolar abscess formation
qs.e: Duct ectasia is typically seen in older multiparous women and is not associated with smoking, whereas periductal mastitis is strongly linked to smokers. Both can present with periareolar masses, but duct ectasia features thick white nipple discharge rather than recurrent painful abscesses.
qs.s: Breast Inflammation: Mastitis, Periductal Mastitis & Duct Ectasia: MCQs

qs.q: When granulomatous mastitis is identified as being idiopathic or autoimmune in origin, what is the standard primary medical treatment?
o: High-dose systemic anticoagulation
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
Steroids
Broad-spectrum oral antifungals
qs.e: Idiopathic or autoimmune granulomatous mastitis is treated with steroids to suppress the aberrant immune response. Antibiotics are reserved for cases proven to have a bacterial or Corynebacterial etiology.
qs.s: Breast Inflammation: Mastitis, Periductal Mastitis & Duct Ectasia: MCQs

qs.q: What is the primary histological feature that defines granulomatous mastitis?
o: Replacement of normal breast adipose tissue by proliferating fibrous scar tissue.
Neutrophil and lymphocyte infiltration directly destroying duct basement membranes.
Lipid‑laden macrophages accumulating inside markedly dilated lactiferous ducts.
Aggregates of activated macrophages forming granulomas within the breast tissue.
qs.e: Granulomatous mastitis is defined by the immune system forming granulomas, which are collections of activated macrophages, within the breast tissue. Accumulation of macrophages inside dilated ducts describes duct ectasia.
qs.s: Breast Inflammation: Mastitis, Periductal Mastitis & Duct Ectasia: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following clinical features is typically absent in duct ectasia, helping to differentiate it from acute mastitis?
o: It commonly occurs in multiparous female patients.
Pain together with prominent overlying skin redness is absent.
A palpable periareolar mass may be present.
Abnormal fluid discharge from the nipple may be observed.
qs.e: Unlike acute mastitis, pain and redness are uncommon in duct ectasia because it is a degenerative condition rather than an active bacterial infection. Both conditions can involve palpable masses and nipple changes.
qs.s: Breast Inflammation: Mastitis, Periductal Mastitis & Duct Ectasia: MCQs
